messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi Mensah is a 37-year-old Ghanaian-American psychologist, currently single, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 61 following a sexual assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. The assault took place during a professional conference, when a colleague invited Kofi to review materials in a hotel meeting room. Once inside, the colleague locked the door. Kofi, who had known this man for several years, did not immediately register the danger. What followed was a rape that lasted, by his estimate, under twenty minutes — a duration he has since found grotesquely disproportionate to its consequences. The locked door, the man's physical proximity, the overheard conversation at the hotel bar about a news story involving sexual violence — all of it was woven into the fabric of those minutes in a way that left each element permanently charged.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi told no one. He is a psychologist who specialises in trauma, and he understood, with a clinician's precision, exactly what was happening to him — which made it no easier to bear, and in some ways considerably worse. He returned to his practice at a university counselling centre, where he sees students in small offices with doors that close. He began leaving his office door ajar during sessions, citing ventilation. When a facilities request required him to meet with a male colleague in a room whose door locked automatically, he experienced a surge of panic so acute he terminated the meeting early and attributed it to a scheduling conflict. The locked room had become unbearable — not as a metaphor, but as a physical fact. The click of a latch, the absence of visible exit, the sense of enclosure: these were no longer neutral sensory events.

What made the threat feel constant was not only the environment but the conclusions Kofi had drawn about himself. He had come to believe, with a certainty that resisted every cognitive intervention he might have offered a patient, that he was permanently exposed — that colleagues, students, even strangers could see the assault written on him simply by looking. This conviction that others could read what had happened to him kept the sense of threat continuously elevated; he could not enter a room, including his own office, without scanning it as though danger were already present. He felt he needed his back against a wall where he could see the full space around him, and he rearranged his office furniture accordingly, placing his chair against the rear wall — a change his supervisor noticed and asked about. He could not relax even at home, even alone, because the belief that he was fundamentally marked and unprotected meant no environment registered as genuinely safe. This same appraisal of helplessness — the settled conviction that he could not prevent bad things from happening to him — fed directly back into his hypervigilance, tightening it: if he could not stop harm, then the only rational response was never to stop watching for it.

The loop between his appraisals and his threat monitoring had become self-sealing. His inability to relax, his sleeplessness, the hours he spent alert in the dark rehearsing exits — all of this confirmed, experientially, that danger was real and ongoing. And because he believed others could see his vulnerability, being alone with male colleagues or clients activated the full constellation of threat responses, making those interactions feel as dangerous as the locked room itself. Comments about sexual violence — a student disclosing an assault, a training podcast, a news headline — landed not as professional content but as direct triggers, pulling him back into the hotel room with an immediacy he could not modulate. His appraisals of hopelessness, the quiet certainty that he had no meaningful future, coloured even these triggered moments: each flashback felt less like an intrusion and more like confirmation.

Kofi sought help only after a student disclosed a sexual assault during a session and he found himself unable to remain clinically present. He excused himself, sat in a bathroom stall for eleven minutes, and later wrote a referral note he described to himself as being in the student's best interest. He knows it was also in his own. What he fears most, coming into treatment, is that the man who understands trauma will be unable to survive his own.
